extracted.intended_audience: students of journalism/media ethics and general readers interested in journalism accountability
extracted.subtask_description: A student-written case analysis of journalistic ethics using the Jayson Blair scandal to illustrate standards, failures, and consequences for journalism and newsroom management. Focuses on ethical principles, verification failures, and institutional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPJ Code of Ethics: honesty, fairness, courage
rubrics_metrics.description: "journalists should be honest, fair and courageous in gathering, reporting and interpreting information." (Society of Professional Journalists’ Code of Ethics)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a foundational standard for journalists — a normative expectation that reporting be truthful, just, and brave in pursuing facts. The essay uses this exact wording to benchmark Blair's conduct against professional norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: There’s an underlying agreement between journalists and the public that the news will be a reliable source of information; the Times changed editorial policy to reflect "a much more cautious, conservative atmosphere... especially [in] verification of reporting."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification includes confirming facts, datelines, sources, and the reporter's presence. The page cites the Times' internal review and policy shift as requiring more rigorous verification to prevent the kinds of inaccuracies Blair produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fabrication and plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Blair was found to be plagiarizing stories and fabricating quotes and datelines; he "lifted material from other newspapers and wire services" and "fabricated quotes and comments."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit prohibition of inventing sources/events or copying others' work; examples given include Blair, Stephen Glass, and Ruth Shalit as precedents of severe ethical breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful representation of location and sourcing (dateline integrity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blair wrote misleading articles by saying he was in other states when he was still in New York and fabricated datelines and on-the-scene presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters must accurately represent where reporting occurred and be able to document presence and sourcing; verifying datelines and on-site reporting is a specific verification task highlighted by the Blair case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize accuracy over style/sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The internal review found Blair gave more importance to style, prose and sensationalism than to accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic value should favor factual correctness and verification above compelling prose or sensational framing; letting style override fact is presented as an anti-pattern that erodes trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, corrections, and internal review
rubrics_metrics.description: The New York Times published a correction article and conducted an internal review that documented problems in many stories (36 out of 73 national stories). The paper called the affair a "low point..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlets should acknowledge errors, correct the record, and perform thorough internal audits when ethical breaches are suspected. Public corrections and explanations are part of restoring accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management oversight and newsroom accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Blair report "exposed a frighteningly porous management structure" that allowed him to thrive; senior editors (Howell Raines and Gerald Boyd) resigned after the scandal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and managers must actively supervise reporters' work, heed warning signs ("warning lights" like repeated inaccuracies), and enforce standards. Lax oversight is identified as a systemic failure enabling individual misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair hiring, promotion practices and avoidance of favoritism
rubrics_metrics.description: Raines was accused by staff of "playing favorites," which may explain Blair's rapid advancement; after the affair the Times reevaluated managing and hiring structure and promoted a more cautious approach to promotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms should ensure promotions and hiring are merit-based and include verification of work quality; favoritism and insufficient vetting of young reporters are cited as enabling factors in the scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve public trust as primary journalistic asset
rubrics_metrics.description: The SPJ case study said the Blair affair severed the trust between the journalist and readers, a necessity if journalism is going to survive; "stories lose their value when the public doesn't trust journalists."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trustworthiness is presented as essential for journalism's social function; ethical breaches reduce audience loyalty and the value of reporting, so decisions should be weighed against their impact on public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical breaches' legal and reputational consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Although "journalistic codes of ethics aren’t legally binding," ethical breaches can be used in court as evidence in libel and privacy cases (example: an attorney invoked the Blair affair in a libel case to undermine journalists' credibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters and organizations should recognize that ethical failures may have downstream legal repercussions and be exploited in litigation and public discourse; maintaining ethical standards can mitigate reputational and legal risks.
